speechtext:
I promised that when I received the
information I would communicate to the house the report of the High Commissioner on the recent conference held in London with respect to wheat. His report, which was received yesterday and decoded this morning, reads as follows:
The final act of the -wheat conference drafted and accepted by all delegates reads:
Final act of the conference of wheat exporting countries held in London at the offices of the High Commissioner for Canada from the 18th day to the 23rd day of May, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-one.
The official delegations of the following countries: America, the United States of; Argentine; Australia; Bulgaria; Canada; Hungary; India; Poland; Roumania; Union of Soviet Socialist Republics; Yugoslavia; have met on the invitation of the Canadian government and at the offices of the High Commissioner for Canada from the 18th May, to the 23rd May, for conference of wheat exporting countries.
The conference invited the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, K.C., etc., High Commissioner for Canada, to act as its chairman. At fourth plenary session on May the 23rd, 1931, the report of the committee was presented to the conference and was finally adopted in the following form:
The conference of wheat exporting coun-tiies, consisting of delegations appointed by the governments of America, the United States of: Argentine: Australia; Bulgaria; Canada:_ Hungary; India; Poland; Roumania; Union of Soviet Socialist Republics; Jugoslavia; having studied existing world wheat situation is con-
World Wheat Conference

vinced that among underlying causes for present depressed prices for wheat, the following points should be specially mentioned:
(i)	'lhe effect of economic depression throughout the world.
(ii)	The fact that there is more wheat produced than can be sold at a profit.
(iii)	The absence of sufficiently adequate information regarding movements of wheat, the requirements of certain countries, and quantities which are liable to be placed upon the market.
(iv)	The present uncertain state of wheat markets.
The conference, recognizing the serious nature of world economic depression, believes nevertheless that a substantial contribution to an improvement of present situation may be made through a clearer understanding of underlying facts regarding so important a commodity as wheat.
The conference considers that, where possible. a reduction in areas devoted to wheat should be undertaken in whatever way each country considers to be most effective and practical.
It was also felt to be especially desirable that there should be careful exploration of all avenues for greater utilization of wheat, both for food and also for other purposes.
The conference further considered current information respecting supply, the demands and the movement of wheat should be brought together in such a way as to assist wheat exporting countries towards orderly marketing of their surpluses.
The conference of wheat exporting countries has. therefore, decided to establish a committee of the conference consisting of one representative from each state participating in the conference to:
(a)	Submit to the governments of the countries participating in this conference a definite proposal for establishing, under supervision of committee of tile conference, a clearing house of information to serve wheat exporting countries. For this purpose, the committee shall be empowered to secure from states represented on committee full information as to unloadings and stock of wheat at all importing points, the areas sown to wheat, and crop prospects, thereby assisting orderly distribution of wheat in world markets. This information should be as far as possible in the form prescribed and at times fixed by committee.
(b)	To explore carefully all possible avenues for greater utilization of this important cereal.
The conference, convinced that existence of this standing committee will develop contacts already established here between wheat exporting countries, proposes that committee may prepare and recommend a draft agenda for a further meeting of conference at which countries here represented may enter upon consideration of subjects as may then be deemed appropriate.
Executed at London, the twenty-third day of May, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-one.

speechtext: This raises a much larger question, namely, whether increases in the tariff are to toe given as a result of confidential information. If any interest is seeking to benefit by an increase in the tariff, such interest ought to be prepared to give to the public all the information necessary to enable the public to judge whether the increase has been given without fear, without favour and in the public interest. That is a very large question, and before rejecting this motion, I hope the Prime Minister will give that phase of the question a little further consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TARIFF BRIEF SUBMITTED TO GOVERNMENT BY DOMINION CARTRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
I have given it consideration. The same question arises frequently before tariff boards in the United States and in this country as well. This subjecting of the cost figures of internal operations of a company to a competitor has never been done in any instance. It is not only unfair, but it is not allowed even in the railway committee in the case of a railway of which we are the shareholders. The right hon. gentleman, I think, confuses two things. The responsibility must be assumed by the government with respect to its tariff legislation, and the method by which it arrives at the legislation may, of course, at times be, as has been said, wholly inaccurate, but it gets the best information it can, sometimes from a tariff board, sometimes from other sources, and sometimes- from both. But I should be loath to believe that the house is of opinion that confidential information connected with the internal economy of the various enterprises in Canada should be made public in the house and thereby benefit a competitor. In this instance the information was given to the government on the distinct understanding that it was not to be subject to publicity. The government, of course, must assume the responsibility for any action it takes, not upon secret information but upon information which is furnished to a cabinet of Canadians who have to consider and deal with the problems in the best way it can. Under our tariff measure now before the house it is not proposed that this information should be made public. The question involves not only this but many other matters of the same character. I am inclined to think upon mature reflection the hon. gentleman himself will see how unfair it would and must be in the very nature of

things to divulge such information when there are competitors-and I shall not go into the question of who they are-who are interested in this particular business and who would be very glad to get this information in this way when they otherwise could not secure it.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS

speechtext:
Mr. A. B. THOMPSON (East Simcoe) moved):
For a copy of all correspondence and other communications in the possession of the government, relating to the preparation of the voters' list for the municipality of Port McNicoll, in the riding of East Simcoe, and a copy of the original list as prepared by the enumerator, and of the revised list as prepared by him for use on election day. Also a copy of any communications exchanged between the chief electoral officer and the returning officer or any other person as to the conduct of the poll on election day.
He said: I desire to say a few words in connection with this resolution standing in my name. I want to enter a protest against the manner in which a number of the electors in my riding were deprived on election day of their right to vote. I claim that a number of the voters in my riding were wrongfully deprived, in connection with the preparation of the voters' list, of their right to vote.
Port McNicoll, for the purpose of the Dominion Elections Act, is a rural municipality, and so the preparation and revision of the voters' list is left in the hands of the local registrar. The registrar prepared his preliminary list, which he posted up in the usual way, and then, in accordance with the provisions of the.act, he proceeded to revise the preliminary list, and then issued his final or
revised list. When his final list was given out, it was found that the registrar had omitted 90 names that he himself had placed on the preliminary list* The registrar in the preparation of this preliminary list is supposed to put on the names of all those whom he believes to be entitled to vote, but when he issued the final list he had taken off 90 names that he himself had put on the preliminary list. The men whose names were struck off received no notice and were given no opportunity to come before the registrar and swear as to their qualifications. They were given no chance at all to prove their right to have a vote. I suppose the reason why this extraordinary power is given to a registrar, there being no appeal from his decision in the matter, is that there is a further provision in the act which says that if the name of a voter in a rural municipality is omitted from the list, the voter may, on election day, go before the deputy returning officer, swear as to his qualifications, be vouched for under oath by a voter already on the list, and then he can demand a ballot. But, sir, Port McNicoll is a lake port town. These men whose names were struck off the list are mariners, forming part of the crews of the four Canadian Pacific steamboats running between Port McNicoll and Fort William. All these boats will not be in port on election day, and in order to give the voters a chance to vote, provision is made in the Act for an advance poll, which under ordinary circumstances would give every one of these men a chance to vote. But, sir, no man can vote at the advance poll unless his name is actually on the list, and so these 90 men-at least from one-half to three-quarters of them-were automatically deprived of the right to vote, because at the most two of these boats, and probably only one, would be in port on election day.
I submit that the elections act should be amended to provide for an appeal from the decision of the registrar, in order that eligible voters such as I have mentioned should not be deprived of their vote. In 1926, with the same number of Canadian Pacific boats in commission and the same number of crews, there were 77 voters who polled their votes at the advance poll. In 1930 this number was reduced to 15, showing conclusively how this thing worked out.
Immediately this revised list was issued by the registrar, my friends directed my attention to it, whereupon I telegraphed to the chief electoral officer. I was in Orillia at the time, right in the midst of my campaign. I wired the chief electoral officer as follows:
Dominion Elections Act

Orillia, July 2, 1930.
Registrar at Port McNicoll in East Simcoe, Ontario, acting under instructions from returning officer, has struck off about 90 voters from list. These men come to Port McNicoll about March, and remain there until end of December, sailing in boats from Port McNicoll to Fort William and return. Many of them unmarried with no other permanent residence. Returning officer justifies his action on letter received from you. Think facts cannot have been properly explained to you. Request that you wire registrar to put these names back on list. Kindly answer me.
A. B. Thompson, M.P.
I received this reply:
Ottawa, July 4, 1930.
Question dealt with in my letter to returning officer related to persons forming crew of Canadian Pacific Railway boats registered in Montreal and plying between Port McNicoll and other ports. Port McNicoll being described as vessels' home port by reason of their spending occasional layover days there. On these facts and assuming individuals concerned continuously housed on board, they are clearly not entitled to vote in Simcoe East. I advised returning officer that only persons really resident in Port McNicoll should be placed on lists for that place.
Jules Castonguay,
Chief Electoral Officer.
On receipt of that telegram I wrote the following letter:
Penetanguishene, Ont.,
July 7, 1930.
Jules Castonguay, Esq.,
Chief Electoral Officer,
Ottawa, Ont.
Re: Port McNicoll Lists
Dear Sir:
In reply to your telegram to me of July 3, I beg to say that the men struck off the list on your instructions go to Port McNicoll about 15th March, and live on shore until about May 15th, when navigation opens and they then go aboard their boats. I consider that every man is entitled to go on the voters' list for some place. I cannot see how these men could go on any other list but that of Port McNicoll, and I claim that these men will have the right to take the oath on election day and be vouched for and vote. To deprive men of their vote is surely not the intention of the act. Some of these men will have to vote at the advance poll. As I read the act, a man's name has to be actually on the list to vote at an advance poll. Is this right, or has he the same right to take the oath as on election day? I would like to hear from you about this point as well.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) A. B. Thompson, M.P.
Then by way of postscript I wrote:
What has the registration of these boats at Montreal to do with the case? They ply between Port McNicoll and Fort William.
To that I received this reply:
Dear Sir,-
I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 7th. The question of the right to vote of persons

employed on the Canadian Pacific steamships was put to me as depending upon whether they could properly be said to be resident in East Simcoe by reason of the fact that Port McNicoll was what was described as their "home port," although not the boat's port of registration, the expression "home port" apparently meaning the port at which the boats lay over between trips, the members of the crew, however, remaining on board. I advised, after consulting with Mr. Biggar, that this casual relationship of the ships to Port McNicoll did not give to the members of the crew who lived upon them the right to describe themselves as "resident" in Port McNicoll or entitle them to vote in Simcoe East as^ having been resident in that electoral district on May 30th inst.
' I have discussed the matter further with Mr. Biggar in the light of your letter under reply and he advised me that the fact that the individuals in question came to Port McNicoll in March and remained there until they joined their ships about the middle of May makes no difference to their qualification assuming that whatever lodgings they had during that interval were, as one would expect, given up upon the ship going into commission, and that thereafter they lived on board. If any particular individuals among them could properly claim to have continued, notwithstanding their having joined their ships, to have retained a residence in Port McNiooll, the conclusion with regard to them might be different, but speaking generally, I suppose it miay be assumed that once they did join their ships their residence ashore ceased.
Only those persons whose names appear on the list are entitled to certificates to vote at an advance poll. The deputy returning officer at an advance poll has no authority to accept any vote from a voter who has not obtained a certificate, and the registrar cannot issue a certificate to anyone whose name has not been included in the list he has prepared.
Yours truly,
Jules Castonguay, Chief Electoral Officer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the chief electoral officer has assumed too much, because as a matter of fact the following are the circumstances. These men start their work on shore about the 15th of March and remain continuously on shore until the 15th of May, when they go aboard their boats. These boats do not occasionally call at Port McNicoll; they call there twice a week. When the navigation season closes these men go ashore again, return to their lodgings and work in the locality until about the end of December. January and February are their holiday months, and they may go away for those two months, but as I said before, they return about the 15th of March. Therefore why these men should be deprived of their right to vote at Port McNicoll is beyond my comprehension, It is the only place where they have any residence, and they could not go on the voting list in any other place.
I may say that I addressed a public meeting at Port McNicoll after the lists were pre-

Dominion Elections Act
pared and after I had had this correspondence with the chief electoral officer. At that meeting I stated that any man whose name had been wrongfully left off the list, and who was in port on election day, had the right to go to the polling booth and demand a ballot, on taking the oath as to his qualifications and on being vouched for by a man whose name was already on the list. That was my advice to the electors, and I believe it to be sound. But, sir, I desire to call attention to what happened on election day, when one of these boats was in port. I have had two affidavits sent to me which I propose reading. The first is by Alexander Campbell and is as follows:
County of Simcoe, and Province of Ontario.
I, Alexander Campbell, of the village of Port 110X10011, in the co-unty of Simcoe,. and the province of Ontario, make oath and say:
That I am 28 years of age, single, and was born in Harris, Invernesshire, Scotland.
That I am employed as a sailor on the SS. Keewaitin sailing between Port MeNicoll and Fort William.
That I have been in Canada since May, 1927, spent one year in Owen Sound, coming to Port McNicoll in 1928. and have resided continuously in Port McNicoll ever since.
That I took a vacation from December 12, 1929, to April 16, 1930, to Harris, Scotland. The previous winter I spent in Port McNicoll, making my home with Bertram Scott, having no other home in Canada.
That on July 28, 1930, I called at the polling booth in Port McNicoll at 2 p.m. and my name not being on the voters' list 1 made application for ballot but was refused by the district returning officer. I returned again at 3 p.m. and took the oath of residence but still the ballot was refused me even with my late landlord to swear to the accuracy of my statement as to residence and on the order of district returning officer Daly I was placed under arrest by the polling booth constable I. Bosley. On Mr. Wm. Finlayson assuming responsibility for my appearance when requested I was released.
That I have heard nothing further about the matter or why I was not allowed to vote after taking the oath of residence.
That the above statement is true, So Help me God.
Sworn before me at Port McNicoll, in the county of Simcoe, and province of Ontario, this 7th day of October, 1930.
Alexander Campbell.
Jas. C. Young,
Notary Public.
The second affidavit is by Fred B. Chid-wick and is in these terms:
County of Simcoe, and province of Ontario.
I, Frederick Benjiman Chidwick, of the village of Port McNicoll, in the county of Simcoe, and the province of Ontario, make oath and say:
That I am 24 years of age, single, and was born in London, England.
That I am employed as a waiter on the SS. Keewatin. sailing between Port McNicoll and Fort William.
That I have resided in Canada since 1922, with the exception of one year vacation in England during 1925.
That I farmed in Shelburne for 15 months prior to shipping on the SS. Alberta in September, 1924, went to England in 1925, returned to Canada in 1926 and shipped on the SS. Assind-boia, In 1927 I shipped on the SS. Keewatin and I have remained a member of the stewards crew through the intervening years.
That during the closed season or winter months I spend some time travelling and visiting other cities but I always consider Port McNicoll my home as I have none other.
That at 10 a.m. on July 28, 1930, I went to the polling place in Port McNicoll, and my name not being on the voters' list I demanded a ballot which was refused me by the district returning officer Daly. I went back twice that afternoon and was finally told that if I could swear to my residence I would be given a ballot. I took the oath but ballot was withheld from me on the advice of Mr. Harvie, a lawyer from Orillia who swore information Against me accusing me of perjury. At the instigation of district returning officer Daly I was placed under arrest by the constable I. Bosley. I was released after Mr. McCormick, general foreman of the Canadian Pacific Railway in Port Mc-Niooll who vouched with Dr. MePhee, for my eligibility to vote became responsible for my appearance to answer the charge preferred against me.
That up to the present time I have heard nothing further about the matter or why I was deprived of exercising my franchise.
That the above statement is true, so help me God.
Fred B. Chidwick.
Sworn before me at Port McNicoll, in the county of Simcoe, and in the province of Ontario, this 7th day of October, 1930.
Jas. C. Young,
Notary Public.
The prosecution of these men was never proceeded with; it was never intended that it should be proceeded with. The idea was to deprive them of their votes, and I want to know if the Dominion Elections Act can be played with in this manner so that honest men are deprived of their votes. I understand that under the common law of England, if a voter is wrongfully refused a ballot the deputy returning officer is liable to damages up to £200, but in Canada, under circumstances such as I have outlined, there is no such responsibility on the deputy returning officer, because our act specially protects him in these circumstances. It says:
Any resident of a rural polling division may vote notwithstanding that his name has been altogether omitted from the list of voters. In any such case the voter must take the oath E on the card, and he must also be vouched for upon oath by some other resident of the polling division whose name is on the voters' list.
Then it concludes as follows:
Thereupon the particulars of the voter whose name was omitted from the voters' list will be added to it with the word "sworn" following,
Dominion Elections Act

and the voter must be given a ballot unless he is immediately proceeded against for perjury; the deputy returning officer has no discretion to refuse the voter a ballot unless a charge is forthwith laid before him.
That is the case here. The English common law gives a man some remedy, on the principle that no wrong can exist without a remedy, but in Canada our elections act takes away from the voter that right. No doubt you are familiar, Mr. Speaker, with that passage from the Bible which says:
Or what man is there of you. whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?
These Canadians asked of their country the right to vote, and what happened? They were arrested. They had a grievance, and they have asked me to bring it before parliament. I have done so, and I leave in the hands of parliament the matter of providing a remedy or affording redress.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not to oppose the motion, because I can see no objection to its being passed, but with the idea that a word or two might well be said to relieve misapprehension as to where responsibility, if any, lie3 for shortcomings in the act or its administration. If the facts aTe -as I am sure they are-as my hon. friend (Mr. Thompson) has represented, it would appear that men who were entitled to vote were prevented from doing so, and that certainly the law either as drafted or as administered should be changed in order to make it quite certain that every citizen shall have the first right of a citizen, namely, to participate in the elections.
The act under which the elections take place is the "act respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise," which is cited as the Dominion Elections Act, 1920. That will make clear to my hon. friend and his friends the time at which the elections, act was drafted in its present form. As I recall it, the act was revised considerably at the time the Union government was in office.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: We have been revising it these last two or three years.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
There have
been some revisions, but I do not think they have touched the essential points brought up in the remarks of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat.
The fact I would like to make clear is this, that the elections act itself, in the main, assumed the form in which it now appears as a result of the important revision which took

place in 1920. Under the act as revised, the business of elections is in the hands of the chief electoral officer, who is an officer of the House of Commons and appointed by this House of Commons. The electoral officer appointed at the time the act was revised was Mr. Oliver Mowat Biggar, whose name has been mentioned by my hon. friend as the legal adviser of the present chief electoral officer. Colonel Biggar was the first chief electoral officer to administer this act as revised, and Colonel Biggar was appointed as a result of a conference, if I remember aright, between the present Minister of Justice and myself, acting together and speaking for the two sides of the house, with a view to securing unanimity with regard to the person who should be chosen as chief electoral officer. All political parties, as a matter of fact, were agreed that Colonel Biggar, having had very much to do with the preparation of the act itself, would be the best possible person to be appointed as chief electoral officer. Mr. Castonguay was appointed assistant electoral officer, and when Colonel Biggar resigned the position, desiring to leave the public service altogether to take up the practice of his profession independently, Mr. Castonguay was by resolution of this house promoted to the position of chief electoral officer.
When the last elections took place the government then in office thought it would be advisable to reassociate Colonel Biggar in some way, if that were at all possible, with the then chief electoral officer, Colonel Biggar being the best informed of >any person in the Dominion with respect to the act and its various provisions, and what should be done with regard to any matters which might come up under its provisions in the course of an election.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Will the right hon. gentleman allow me? Is he attempting to state the reason why Colonel Biggar was made counsel to the chief electoral officer? Does he not know that it was the consensus of opinion of the special committee dealing with the elections act last year and the year before that Mr. Castonguay was not qualified to carry out the provisions of the act?

speechtext:
Where do you get
that?

I know,
because I was there.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is taking a very unfair advantage of any privilege he may have as a member of par-

Dominion Elections Act
liament to attack a member of the civil service who is not here in a position to defend himself.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I am not doing anything that I did not do to Mr. Castonguay's face last year and the year before, in the committee.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
There is a
great deal of difference between saying something to a man's face when he is in a position to reply, and taking advantage of the privilege which one has as a member of parliament to make statements which I submit should not be made by any hon. member, seeing that they constitute an attack upon a member of the civil service, who is also an officer of this House of Commons but who is not in a position in any way to defend himself. However, the point is quite clear, that Mr. Castonguay came to the office of chief electoral officer by promotion and by unanimous resolution of this house, having been assistant to Colonel Biggar when Colonel Big-gar was chief electoral officer, and that he had as legal adviser, Colonel Biggar who was in a better position to advise on matters respecting the elections act than any other individual.
Now with respect to this case at Port Mc-Nicoll which has been referred to, the hon. member has read telegrams which would indicate that Mr. Castonguay, the chief electoral officer, had referred the specific questions at issue to Colonel Biggar for his advice, and that he secured and acted upon the advice of Colonel Biggar, so I assume no better course possibly could have been taken. If the advice was not sound, that is a matter for discussion and might well be brought up when the elections act is being considered, but I can think of no one who would be in a better position to advise soundly on any matter pertaining to the elections act than Colonel Biggar, not only from the circumstance that he, more than any other single person, had to do with its drafting, and himself had acted as chief electoral officer, but also because he is a very eminent counsel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: It is difficult to understand his advice.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says it is difficult to understand his advice. That possibly may be so; that is a matter which I would prefer that lawyers settle among themselves, but what I do submit is ihat with respect to the course taken by the chief electoral officer, it is not open to criticism. He took the precaution to consult Colonel Biggar, and then in the matter acted upon his advice.
The act, as I have said, was passed in 1920 and the pertinent provisions with regard to the chief electoral officer are as follows:
The chief electoral officer shall be appointed by resolution of the House of Commons-
That was done with respect to both electoral officers whose names have been mentioned. Then subsection Ob) provides that he, the electoral officer, shall:
exercise general direction and supervision over the administrative conduct of elections with a view to ensuring the fairness and impartiality of all election officers and compliance with the provisions of this act;
(c) report to the House of Commons, through the Speaker, after an election, any matters arising in the course of the election an account of which ought, in his judgment, to be submitted to the House of Commons.
The point I wish to make clear in this connection is that parliament itself has sought to remove and has removed from the possible control of any political party or any government in office the administration of the Dominion Elections Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Was this point referred to? I cannot remember, looking through the report, that the chief electoral officer mentioned this point.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
I do not know of its having been mentioned, but it seems to me that the particular matter that has been brought up to-day is one that properly would come within the kind of report which the chief electoral officer might be expected to make to the Speaker of the House of Commons. As to the question whether oi not this matter was brought by the chief electoral officer to the attention of His Honour the Speaker, I would point to another section of the act which touches specifically upon the rights of parties concerned as respects references to be made to the Speaker by the chief electoral officer. Section 75 reads:
The chief electoral officer shall, after each election, make a report to the Speaker of the House of Commons, suggesting what, if any, amendments are in his opinion desirable for the more convenient administration of the law, and each candidate and the agent of each candidate shall have the right to send written statements to the chief electoral officer suggesting such changes and improvements in the law as to such person may deem desirable, and to make written complaint of the conduct of any officer employed an such election.
Any such statements and complaints shall be transmitted by the chief electoral officer to the said Speaker, and they shall, together with the report of the chief electoral officer, be forthwith submitted by the said Speaker to the House of Commons if parliament is then sitting, and if not, within fifteen days after the opening of the next session of parliament.
Dominion Elections Act

I do not know whether my hon. friend who has just spoken did forward a written statement to the chief electoral officer, suggesting such changes and improvements in the law as to him seemed desirable, and making a written complaint of the conduct of the officer employed in the election. That, I submit, is a step which he would not only have been justified in taking but which he should have taken in a matter of this kind, because as a member of parliament he is interested, as he has shown this afternoon, in bringing to the attention of parliament any deficiencies that exist in the law and in making suggestions as to possible remedies. I am inclined to think that my hon. friend's reason for waiting to bring up the matter in the form in which he has introduced it this afternoon has been due mainly to his desire to make the speech which he has made, and which he has made I think in a very moderate and acceptable way. So far as the remedy to meet such a situation is concerned, the act itself provides, as I now read, that a member of parliament or a candidate may bring to the attention of the chief electoral officer, with a view to having it submitted to His Honour the Speaker, any defect in the law of a character such as has been mentioned to-day. Had that course been pursued, we should not have had to wait until the 25th of May to have knowledge of what took place at Port McNicoll; it would have been the duty of His Honour the Speaker to report the matter at the opening of the house.
I see no reason why the request of my hon. friend for all the information should not be complied with; but I do not think except for the desired publicity there is any reason why he should have made the speech he made this afternoon. In view of what has been said I do see strong reason why just what the act provides should be made clear, lest an inference be drawn from my hon. friend's remarks that the government which was in office at the time of the election was in any way responsible for any defect or deficiency in the law. The act itself was passed by a previous administration, and the chief electoral officer was an officer of the House of Commons, chosen by unanimous resolution of the house. He has sole control of the administration of the act; and, in exercising his functions, he pursued the wisest and best course and was governed by the wisest and best advice which was obtainable. If, in spite of that, someone seems to have been deprived of the right of voting, then it does seem that, obviously, when the act comes to be amended, some remedy should be pro-
vided to meet a situation such as that which has been described. And if there are cases of that character, the sooner the act is amended in that particular, the better.

subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: What remedy would my hon. friend suggest for the men who were arrested?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BIGHT OF APPEAL SUGGESTED IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
The inference which I drew from the statement made to the house by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Thompson) was that something was seriously wrong in regard to the vo.tes of these ninety men at Port McNicoll during the last election, and I believe it is the duty of the House of Commons in a case like this to endeavour to fix the blame-because blame there was somewhere. Either, Colonel Biggar, the legal adviser of the chief electoral officer, was not fully informed, or he was misinformed. I cannot conceive of his giving the advice which he did give if the facts were as related by the hon. member for East Simcoe to-day-and I believe the facts were fairly related to the house. Ninety men have as a result been deprived of their votes, and a very serious situation has arisen in regard to that poll.
It would appear that certain information passed from the constituency of East Simcoe to the chief electoral officer, of which we are not aware, because it is certain that information went to the constituency of East Simcoe to have warrants issued, ready to apprehend any person of these ninety who should appear and ask for a ballot, or seek to vote. And the two residents of Port McNicoll who did appear at the polling place and who demanded the right to take the oath and vote were immediately arrested. The warrants were there. The case had been prearranged under someone's authority and instructions, and it was only on the intercession of the Hon. William Finlayson, a member of the Ontario government, that these persons were subsequently released. It looks to me as though there were more in this case than appears on the surface.
We have a tribunal in this house specially charged with the investigation of matters of this kind when they are referred to it; that is, the standing committee of the House of Commons with respect to privileges and elections. I do not know that it would be very much satisfaction to my hon. friend from East Simcoe or to the ninety men who were deprived of the right to exercise their franchise on the 28th day of July last, if the hon. member for East Simcoe should merely write a letter to the chief electoral officer,' suggesting some amendment in the

Marine Insurance
law. If a wrong has been done it is our duty to investigate it. On the face of it, I am inclined to think that some kind of conspiracy has existed to deprive these particular men of their votes on election day. My suggestion to my right hon. friend and to the house is that the motion carry, that the papers be produced, and that if they bear out in any way the case which has been made by the hon. member for East Simcoe the matter be referred to the committee on privileges and elections in order that a thorough investigation may be made.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION

speakeroldname: Mr. A. E. ROSS (Kingston City) moved:
subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
That the continuation of navigation after November 1st. on the great lakes has taken a great toll from the lives of our mariners and while this dangerous period of navigation is continued as a national necessity and is yearly undertaken by a courageous marine body, this house deems it the duty of the federal government to provide insurance for each mariner on Canadian boats from November 1st, to the end of navigation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, to any hon. member who represents a constituency the residents of which are largely mariners this motion will be of interest and should receive sympathy. From the first reading of the motion it might appear to be out of order in that it asks the federal government to provide insurance, .but if the house will bear patiently with my remarks I hope to show that it is not out of order on that ground. It might appear also to be out of order because of possible interference with the privileges and rights of the provinces, but I hope to be able to show that this is not a provincial matter.
The period of navigation referred to in this motion is a very dangerous one on the great lakes. I think it was in the year 1902 that a well-known steamer, the Bannockburn, disappeared with all on board. No information respecting that disaster has been obtained up to the present time. Twenty-two lives were lost, mostly men from the city of Kingston. Other disasters have since occurred, practically all during this dangerous period. Other steamships cease to operate on or about November 1, but these boats engaged in the transport of grain carry on later than that. The carrying of grain is a national necessity and is therefore a matter of concern to the federal parliament.
Certain measures have been adopted which have effected considerable improvement with
respect to this matter. I am proud to say that the province of Ontario has dealt with it most sympathetically. The compensation act of Ontario contains this clause:
Where an accident happens out of Ontario on a steamboat, ship or vessel or on a railway and the workman is a resident of Ontario and the work or service rendered by him is required to be performed both within and without Ontario, the workman or his dependents shall be entitled to compensation under this part as if the accident had happened in Ontario.
In the summary on compensation issued by the Labour department in January, 1931, the following reference is made to this legislation:
The Ontario and Manitoba acts include within their scope the operation of steam vessels and works for the purposes of the business of a navigation company and all other navigation, towing, operation of vessels and marine wrecking, but in Ontario the employer in these industries is individually liable.
My intention in introducing this motion is to bring to the attention of the house and of whatever department it may pertain to- I am not sure what department will be affected-the fact that this matter should be placed beyond any doubt. We have listened to-day to a discussion on what residence means, and if the same doubt exists in regard to the payment of compensation to mariners or their dependents, it would be impossible for them to go into court and testify as to their rights.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Has the hon. member any information with regard to whether or not other provinces pay such compensation?

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
That is one of the reasons
for my bringing up this motion. I know no decision can be given to-day, but the matter should be discussed in order that we may obtain information as to how the other provinces are treating this matter. Last year the province of Quebec accepted the same standards as those applying in the province of Ontario, at least I have been so informed, but many of these steamship companies have their headquarters in other parts of the Dominion and for the sake of the mariners who are engaged in this hazardous work at the dangerous period referred to, there should be no doubt as to where they stand in regard to the payment of compensation when disasters occur.
This matter is or can be made a federal one. The committee on industrial and international relations brought down in 1926 a ruling which still stands, as follows:
Local works and undertakings, other than such as are of the following classes (a) lines
Marine Insurance

of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting a province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province; (b) lines of steamships between the provinces and any British or foreign country, such works as although wholly situated within the province, are before or after their execution, declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or to the advantage of two or more of the provinces.	[DOT]
So that the matter can be made a federal one, and I think those of us who represent those ports on the great lakes where so much suffering has been caused in the past by marine disasters will take a sympathetic view of the question and will place it in the hands of some committee or some department of the house where action may be taken so that there may no longer 'be any doubt with respect to it.
A short time ago the house was sjunpathetic to a former motion of mine, and I am sure the present motion will command the same sympath}' from all parts of the house, having regard to the fact that many constituencies, town and ports that may be concerned are represented here. It may be that some hon. member may have in his constituency a man whose residence may be disputed, but who either has lost his life or may yet lose his life in carrying on this important work, and whose dependents may receive compensation or insurance on that account.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Farmers engaged in the
business to which my hon. friend refers-that is, transporting grain in the winter, but transporting it across the prairies-have been overtaken by a snowstorm and lost their way, and their remains have later been found under a snowdrift. Would my hon. friend be willing to extend insurance to those men also?

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: I suppose in such a case the wheat belongs to the farmer. The ruling has already been given that if a man owns any part of the boat which goes down, he cannot claim compensation. Even with the law as it is at the present time, if a man takes wheat on a steamboat, the ruling would be against the man who owned the wheat.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
What about the farmer's
hired man?

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member is at all backward about introducing legislation and looking after it. If he will attend to that, I am attending to this.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Do I understand that these mariners are navigating at their own risk?

Mr. RO'SS: No, but after November, the insurance rates on boats are very greatly increased. I may be asked why I do not bring in a motion requiring the owners of steamboats to provide this compensation. I have no power to do this with regard to owners of steamboats. The steamboat is insured ; the grain is insured; everything is insured except the human life involved in the transportation. We have no power to go after the steamboat companies unless the government can take this action, and that is why I am bringing the matter to the attention of the federal government.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Under the practice that prevails can the seamen take out insurance themselves?

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: The captains, mates and so forth do, but the deckhands do not.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVISION FOR CANADIAN MARINERS ON GREAT LAKES FROM NOVEMBER 1 TO END OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Although representing a constituency which, since it is far from the ports, contains no considerable number of mariners, I am sympathetically interested in this motion. I do represent a constituency, 'however, which has to do largely with grain growling and grain shipping, and to us every day of navigation at the end of the season is a matter of deep concern. It is important to us, and I think to the country, that the shipment of grain should be carried on until the very last possible moment, and we realize quite well that during the last days of navigation before the season closes there .must of necessity 'be much danger to the men engaged in that work. Without going into the matter at length, I wish to say merely this: with regard to the constitutional aspect I am not certain where the onus of responsibility should lie. I am not sure just how this should be done, but in the national interest, in the interest not only of those who carry the grain, but of those who are anxious to see that grain carried until as late in the year as possible, I am convinced that this matter should be given most sympathetic attention. 'Certainly we should consider whether it is possible for parliament to see to it that those who imperil their lives in a national service of this kind should at least be secured so far as they can be, by some form of insurance. If it cannot be done privately; if it is not the duty of the province, then I for one, should be glad to see the federal government and parliament take the matter into consideration, and if possible accede to some measure such as that suggested in the resolution.

That can readily be done, as was suggested to this house some years ago, by the government fixing a date on which navigation on the great lakes would close in the fall. Human greed will always take a risk, with somebody else's life, and have boats laden with grain go out on the great lakes after it has ceased to be safe for them to do so owing to the weather, the make of the boat perhaps, and the way she is loaded. I would suggest that it would be more to the point if we safeguarded not the money point of view, but the lives of our mariners by giving power to this government to proclaim, after due investigation a date in the fall on which navigation must close. Not necessarily. Now,
if our deliberations are loyal and patriotic they will harmonize with the splendid history of the empire, and we, Canadians and Britishers, always venerate our great national, political, imperial and religious heritage. Realizing the great contributions to civilization that have been made by the British Empire, we shall by sane and sensible advocacy safeguard, unify, extend and symbolize the great ideas for which the British Empire stands-here in Canada our national home.
The people of the Dominion from one ocean to the other are watching this debate. All loyal and patriotic Canadians will be anxious to learn the reception of this resolution at the hands of hon. members and the Prime Minister. This being Victoria or Empire day, it is perhaps the most fitting day for a discussion of such a resolution; the discussion is also appropriate in view of the fact that this is the first regular session of the seventeenth parliament of Canada. On this remembrance day, when we should remember the undying splendours and imperishable legacies handed down to us from the Victorian era; when we should remember our responsibilities and our duties to Canada and the empire, and when we should rededicate and reconsecrate ourselves to that continuous labour for freedom, without which freedom is not won, it seems to me the time for our discussion is rather short, but that with a further discussion permitted later on we may be able to go into the subject more fully.
Now, on this day of empire, there are certain calls that come to us, calls of love for the God of nations, honour to the king, obedience to the law, advancement of the highest interests of the empire in peace and war, the cherishing of patriotism, the paying of scrupulous regard to the rights of other nations, the mastery of the principles of citizenship, the following of duty, the acquiring of knowledge, the practice of discipline, the work for others and the considering of the poor and afflicted. These are the commands that come to us on this empire day, the watchwords of which are responsibility, duty, sympathy and self-sacrifice.
With regard to the resolution, Mr. Speaker, which stands in my name on the order paper, might I say that it was inspired by my own national conception of Canada, and that it was not inspired by any province making up Canada. It did not come from Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick or Quebec or Ontario or Saskatchewan, or any other province making up this Dominion.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR ADOPTION OF FLAG SYMBOLIC OF CANADA AND HER PARTNERSHIP IN BRITISH EMPIRE
speechtext:
Or from Winnipeg
either. It will be seen that the resolution is made up of five major parts. First, the opinion of the house is required on this important resolution; second, a special committee should be appointed to deal with the question, just as the government deals with other resolutions, not only with regard to government measures but also coming from private members; third, the advisability of adopting a Canadian flag; fourth, choosing a suitable symbol to stand for Canada in the flag, and fifth, the placing of the union jack in the union or position of honour to indicate our allegiance to the British crown. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that eighty or ninety per cent of the people of Canada are favourable to this action, and the opposition that comes to this progressive move on the part of the Dominion comes only from a few noisy individuals and a few noisy organizations. The same noisy individuals and organizations will fight us if we decide to amend our constitution; they will fight us as they have fought us in days gone by in the evolution of government, and we may expect their opposition in days to come in any progressive step in the direction of adopting a national flag for Canada, but I do not think we need pay very much attention to opposition of that kind. I believe this flag should represent Canada as a political unit, made up of nine provinces reaching from sea to sea, with the union jack occupying the position of honour -that is the vital position; that is the position of union in that flag, thereby showing the cooperation of Canada with the motherland in the building up of our empire and in making it more permanent than ever.
This being the case, Mr. Speaker, it might be well to say a few words on the Dominion of Canada, with which this resolution is concerned in the way of a national flag. Canada has been defined as consisting of three thousand miles of territory made up of one thousand miles of inland lake and river and sea, plus one thousand miles of boundless prairie, plus one thousand miles of mountain. That is the land from the border northward which is being extended day by day; that is the land for which we want a Canadian flag. Again, Canada has been defined as a mighty potential giant, the head of which rests upon the broad Pacific, whose arms make up the Rockies and the Selkirks, whose body is the great plains of the west and whose limbs are the two great water

A Canadian Flag
systems, the St. Lawrence and Hudson bay. Our duty, as Canadians, is to develop and make out of that giant on the northern shoulder of this continent one of the great nations of the world. And we will do it.
What do the poets say about this great Dominion, this young giant, this Canada, our native land? Poets have a habit of saying a thing and saying it well. Here is what Charles G. D. Roberts, one of our leading poets in the maritimes, says:
O Child of Nations, giant-limbed,
Who stand'st among the nations now
Unheeded, unadored, unhymned,
With unanointed brow,-
The Saxon force, the Celtic fire,
These are thy manhood's heritage!
Why rest with babes and slaves? Seek higher The place of race and age.
O Falterer, let thy past convince Thy future,-all the growth, the gain,
The fame since Cartier knew thee, since Thy shores beheld Champlain!
Montcalm and Wolfe! Wolfe and Montcalm! Quebec, thy storied citadel
Attests in burning song and psalm How here thy heroes fell!
Then in rising splendour the last verse:
But thou, my country, dream not thou! Wake, and behold how night is done,-
How on thy breast, and o'er thy brow,
Bursts the uprising sun!
The uprising sun of freedom and of nationhood. Surely in this Canada of the present day we ought to have a flag, of a national and a Canadian nature, that will symbolize our Dominion throughout the world. Surely! Then what does Pauline Johnson say about Canada? Here are a few lines by Pauline Johnson:

(Acrostic)
C rown of her, young Vancouver; crest of her, old Quebec;
A tlantic and far Pacific sweeping her, keel to deck.
N orth of her, ice and arctics; southward a rival's stealth;
A loft, her Empire's pennant; below, her nation's wealth,
D aughter of men and markets, bearing within her hold,
A ppraised at highest value, cargoes of grain and gold.
Then again Pauline Johnson shows the association of Canada with the empire, in her poem entitled "Canadian Bom":
We first saw light in Canada, the land beloved of God;
AVe are the pulse of Canada, its marrow and its blood:	.
And we, the men of Canada, can face the world and brag
That we were born in Canada beneath the British flag.
And lastly Grant Balfour says-and these lines are also beautiful, I think:
Dominion of the North, how vast; Unequalled in the distant past By proud imperial Rome.
The sister zones o'er thee unrolled Two giant belts of white and gold Fair Canada, my home.
It is for this fair Canada, my home, that I am not afraid to stand up this afternoon and tell the members of this house and the people of Canada that the time has arrived when we should, in association with the other selfgoverning units of the empire, have a typical national or Canadian flag.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me come to the imperial conferences of 1926, 1929 and 1930. At the imperial conference of 1926 a certain amount of splendid work, imperially and nationally, was accomplished, and the work of that conference and the conference of 1929 has been practically endorsed by the conference of 1930. This being the case, it might be well for us to consider for a moment just what that means. In the summary of the proceedings of the conference of 1926 we have the following statement:
There is, however, one most important element in it which, from a strictly constitutional point of view, has now, as regards all vital matters, reached its full development- we refer to the group of self-governing communities composed of Great Britain and the Dominions.
Their position and mutual relation may be leadilly defined. They are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
Further on the statement is made:
And though every Dominion is now, and must always remain, the sole judge of the nature and extent of its cooperation, no common cause will, in our opinion, be thereby imperilled.
In other words, the day has arrived in the history of the empire when there is no longer force or compulsion; and if there is any appearance of compulsion it is only in form and not in fact or reality.
This empire of ours is, of course, the greatest the world has ever seen. It is not a centralized empire; constitutionally it is rather a decentralized one. And since it is decentralized it would, of course, be impossible to have what we might call a federation of the empire because of the differences in characteristics, the varying stages of evolution, the wide spaces geographically dividing one section from another, and our different histories. The pathway to empire greatness, empire solidarity and empire permanency that of self-govern-
A Canadian Flag

ment or autonomy, founded on positive and not on negative ideals, is therefore the pathway to greatness and security.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that free cooperation and free institutions are the life blood of the empire. Free cooperation is the instrument which makes possible the functioning of its different parts, and the high objectives ever before the empire, of peace, prosperity and security, will most assuredly lead us into greater epochs than we have known in the past. Since there is an entire absence of compulsion in empire building, it means that from now on the empire must adjust itself to new conditions, and new conditions must become subordinate to new ideals.
That brings me to the question of the Union Jack, the flag of the United Kingdom- in other words, the red, white and blue, which signify all that is brave, pure and true, and what it symbolizes in the life of the empire. The Union Jack is the flag of the United Kingdom. It is made up of three crosses, St. George's, St. Andrew's and St. Patrick's, eight blue triangles plus white borders, all of which .is fraught with sacred meaning to the citizens of the empire.
Now, as regards these patron saints, whose lives typify great sacrifice, it might be well to realize just what the flag has stood for in the past. The flag in history has stood for the following:
The flag of the great union of Scotland and England up to 1603, and since 1707 and 1801- the Union Jack, floated on high when the victorious Marlborough went from victory to victory in France and Spain in the war of the Spanish succession.
It was the settled flag of the union when Bonnie Prince Charlie struck for Stuart power once more in Scotland.
It was the flag of Scotland and England when Walpole was named for the first time Prime Minister of Britain.
It waved in the breeze during the Seven Years' war in India, Europe and America; at Plassey, Rossbach, and over Wolfe and his men at the plains of Abraham; battles in which the supremacy of Britain was settled on three continents for good.
It stood for greater freedom of thought and expression when Wilkes dared the authorities in the last half of the eighteenth century to stem his criticism of the government of the day without which liberty of opinion would not have been able all along t'he line for generations to make democracy as stabilized as it is at present.
It blew in the breeze at Trafalgar, Corunna, Waterloo and Khartum, over Nelson, Sir John Moore and Wellington and Gordon.

It was the flag of the United Empire Loyalists and the other bands of courageous pioneers in the wilds of the Canadas and the maritimes when the Canada of the future was taking form on the northern shoulder of the new world.
It was the symbol of the French Canadians of Quebec when they fought with superb courage for local liberty in 1812 against the United States.
It was thrown to the winds of France when the French Canadians led the van at Cour-celette for world freedom.
It waves over India, after centuries of bloodshed and oppression; over the sands of the Soudan, the historic monuments of Egypt, over the cedars of Mount Lebanon, over the hilltops of Palestine, the plains of Mesopotamia and the as yet untamed regions of the northern world and Antarctic wastes.
It was the emblem of freedom that stemmed the advance of tyranny in the world war, and still sweeps the seas in the interests of world peace, world development and world progress and cooperation.
I have described what the flag has stood for in history. Let me now say what it stands for among the nations. It further stands for:
International honour.
National liberty.
Individual freedom.
Empire fellowship.
Maintenance of law and order under democratic institutions.
Constitution in which every man and woman has a voice, in accordance with franchise acts that will in time, we hope, be modernized to the last limit of representative and responsible government requirements.
A system of monarchy providing a vita! link of peace, progress, cooperation and unity among the nations making up the British commonwealth of nations circling the globe.
The traditions and history of the British race in peace, commerce, art, science, literature, law, education, industry and war.
Symbol of the common sentiment animating the British people throughout the centuries.
Rallying point of the common force during the emergency periods in our racial development and without which defeat would have rendered impossible a destiny potentially equal to, if not the superior of, any other world power.
The symbol of law, order and discipline in all military and naval movements, making possible the extension of our empire frontiers from century to century.

A Canadian Flag
Past resolves, past deeds and past heroes, apart from which the finest enthusiasm on behalf of home, family pride, family honour, personal devotion, patriotism or religious zeal; all of. which, in addition to leadership, numerical forces and discipline have been needed in the past to wrench victory from many a haughty and gallant foe.
Distinguishing mark of armies, fleets, departments of government, parties, rulers, officers, families, clans, dominions, kingdoms, empires, commonwealths and nations.
National growth, power, influence, unity and advancement in the cause of liberty.
National pride, glory, honour and protecting power from wrong, within and without our empire and nation's boundaries.
The unity of ideals and righteousness imperially and nationally which shall unite the world in freedom and justice.
And what about a Canadian flag? A Canadian flag would stand for all these things, since Canada is a self-governing unit in the British commonwealth of nations, and for many more-the developments in Canada since 1801.
The vicissitudes and upheavals nationally from -which we have emerged as a portion of the British Empire prior to and subsequent to confederation.
The stirring history of centuries when early Canada was under the influence and sovereignty of imperial France, and when in navigation, exploration, discovery and colonization the foundation work of the Canada to be was grappled with in a spirit of unparalleled courage and devotion.
Institution of representative and responsible government as factors in the development of the country internally, imperially and internationally.
Canada, the Canadian people, their aspirations and visions of continental and world greatness.
The crown and the laws that bind us by golden chains in allegiance to the throne of Britain.
That spirit of sacrifice and sendee which in the late great war brought so many of our men to national consciousness and manhood, and caused so many of them to express a sincere desire for a nationally distinctive emblem.
The further sacrifices comparable with anything in the way of sacrifice in the history of pioneers; sacrifices of the intrepid French missionaries and martyrs of early Canadian history, British missionaries of the Cross, and the mutual sacrifice, courage, cooperation, service, forbearance, devotion and Canadian and
British comradeship that must characterize us as a people if we are to aspire to and attain the great objectives placed wdthin our reach by a thoughtful and beneficial Providence.
All these things would a Canadian flag stand for-a Canada up to date and yet to be.
And may I point out now, Mr. Speaker, that New Zealand, Australia, South Africa and Newfoundland have flags of their own, and India will have a flag of its own under its new constitution. Ireland has a flag of its own and so, I believe, have all the self-governing dominions of the empire. The question then arises, what about Canada?
Mr. LaVERGNE:	We had a flag of our
own in 1904.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR ADOPTION OF FLAG SYMBOLIC OF CANADA AND HER PARTNERSHIP IN BRITISH EMPIRE
speechtext:
I am coming to that.
What about Canada? We have now a king closer than ever constitutionally, therefore dearer than ever. We have a royal standard which suggests the United Kingdom. We have an empire flag; we have a British white ensign; a British blue ensign and a British red ensign. We have a new governor general's flag, not made up of the union jack as if was a few years ago, but made up in an entirely different way because the governor general now represents His Majesty and not the British government. How terrible our super-loyalists must feel about this. We have a merchant marine flag which is our flag on the seas, since 1892, simply a red ensign with the arms of Canada in the fly. We have a government service flag, tne British blue ensign with the coat of arms of Canada in the fly. On the government buildings outside of Canada such as in Washington, Paris, London and Tokyo, we fly the red ensign as our Canadian flag. We have therefore a Canadian flag in London, but we have not a Canadian flag in Canada. We have a flag which we fly on the Canadian government buildings in Paris and the other world capitals, but we cannot fly that same flag on our own parliament buildings in the Dominion of Canada. That is the situation exactly.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	We used to.
